title: Pilot Results: A cafeteria food-waste sorting program
text:
The Northbridge Planning Office tested a cafeteria food-waste sorting program. Three schools added labeled sorting stations and short student demonstrations for six weeks. Staff published the following summary after the trial.

RESULTS TABLE
Edible food discarded: 410 kg before | 315 kg during pilot
Contamination in compost bins: 18% before | 9% during pilot
Meals served: 5,820 before | 5,760 during pilot
Students saying labels were easy to understand: 64% before | 86% during pilot

The office warned readers not to treat the largest percentage change as automatically the best outcome. Some measures describe benefits, while others describe costs or side effects. A sound conclusion has to consider the direction of each measure and whether the comparison period was similar enough to make the change meaningful.

Because the number of meals served changed only slightly, the drop in discarded edible food is unlikely to be explained by a major change in cafeteria volume alone. Analysts also checked whether one unusual week was driving the result. Removing that week changed the exact percentages slightly but did not reverse the overall pattern.

Several residents asked why the report included both counts and survey responses. The project manager explained that the two forms of evidence answer different questions. Counts show what happened at the system level, while surveys can reveal how people experienced the change. Neither should automatically replace the other.

The office recommended one more trial before permanent expansion. The next version would keep the same core measurements so results could be compared over time, but it would also add one measure for a concern raised during the first trial. The recommendation was based on the combined pattern, not on a single favorable number.

The situation also shows why interpreting data with text cannot be judged from one isolated detail. People in the passage weigh immediate results against longer-term effects, and they revise their choices as new information becomes available.

Another important feature is the way the evidence is limited. The people involved can observe what happened in this setting, but they cannot assume the same outcome would occur everywhere. That distinction matters when readers decide how strongly a conclusion is supported.

The passage repeatedly connects decisions with consequences. Some effects are measured directly, while others are described through observations or testimony. Readers therefore have to separate what the text states from what it only suggests.

By the end, the central question is not whether every concern disappears. It is whether the available evidence is strong enough to justify the next step while leaving room to correct the plan if later results differ.
